segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Susanna and Margaret were close. It was a real friendship and a work friendship. They talked four or five times a week, every week for the last 18 years.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: We would start talking about some work piece of business. And then we would digress into a combination of motherly advice from her and gossiping, which would last for 30 to 45 more minutes. She had a lot of advice, and she didn't mince her words about what I was doing wrong. She also was very loving and there for me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Margaret died on Tuesday. Margaret Riley is her name. She was somebody who managed screenwriters and directors and actors, too. She was 58. Susanna is Susanna Fogel, one of her clients. And she says the remarkable thing about Margaret is how up until the end, she kept hidden how sick she was. The cancer had returned. It was a secret from nearly everybody.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: Even if you pushed and asked, she would not divulge that piece of it. Like, I had texted her and said, hey, I feel like we just talk about trivial stuff. And can we talk about your health? And she said, I actually love to be distracted from talking about my health. Let's talk about you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: And she would do that a lot.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Margaret didn't want to get into it. She wanted to engage with people the way she always had. She liked working. She wanted to keep at it the way she was used to. And that continued literally until the day she died, Tuesday this week. Doctors had already told her that she didn't have much time. She was getting hospice care at home.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: And so on Monday and Tuesday, she had a series of Zoom meetings, notes calls, calls with writers, calls with executives. And she refused to let anybody cancel them, and she refused to let people come and see her when she was booked into these professional meetings, which she attended.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In fact, the day Margaret died, her mother was flying to LA to see her.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: So there was a race for her to get from the airport in time to say goodbye. But in the meantime, that same day, Margaret was confirming and insisting that she be part of these Zooms. She didn't want to cancel any of that. So at the very end, her assistant had to lie to her and tell her that the meetings were canceled so that she wouldn't try to kick people out of her room so that she could Zoom about a project. It could have prevented her from saying goodbye to somebody that needed to see her.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Susanna was in that situation because just a few days before Margaret died, somebody in Margaret's inner circle confided in her just how bad things were, which Margaret very much did not want her to know. And Susanna couldn't just rush to see her because she was at a film festival, at Sundance showing a film that she and Margaret had spent five years trying to get made. And Saturday was the premiere.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: And so I was engaging with Margaret throughout the weekend. Every time we texted, I wanted to stop this performance that things were fine and just tell her that I knew what was going on and tell her everything I wanted to tell her, even if it was in a text message. But I also knew that she had really wanted to engage as though things were normal. So there's a series of text messages we sent to each other where I'm kind of poking around the idea that I want her to let me know what's really going on, and she's refusing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Do you have the text there?

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: Yeah, I do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, can you read them?

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: Mm-hmm. So I texted her a few hours after I got this tip from this friend of hers that she was, you know, at the end. And I said, hey, how are you feeling? She said, today's been good. How's Sundance so far? And I said, fun. I'm nervous. A couple of hours later, she texted just before my screening, good luck this afternoon. Can't wait to hear. Three exclamation points.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It continues from there. Susanna sends a picture of her outfit. Margaret hearts it. Then the film screens.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: And then she knew the running time of the film, and the second the movie was over, she texted me again. How did it go? Three question marks, three exclamation points.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Susanna sends pictures and a review. Her last text to Margaret on Monday, 7:06 PM, is about how she's going to come over as soon as she gets back to LA to gossip and tell her all about Sundance. This was Susanna laying the groundwork to just show up at Margaret's house Tuesday, whether Margaret liked it or not, and get more real. Margaret never answered that text. And Susanna's found herself thinking a lot about what she wanted to say to her, ideally in person, or even in some last text that she could have sent last weekend when she still had the chance.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: I think what's interesting is when I think about what I would have said in a final text message to her, I probably would have said, I don't even have words. I don't think I would have been able to compose a text message that felt like it covered the depth of my love for her. Or the words would have failed, or they wouldn't have been enough or something.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: I would have talked about how words were inadequate, which she would have been very disappointed in because I'm a writer, and you know, she was representing me. But you know.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Right. That's your job.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: Yeah. She would have said, come on, you can do it. Don't be a quitter.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Words can be so puny sometimes in the face of feelings.

segments.speaker: Susanna Fogel
segments.text: Yeah. If I was in person, I probably would have just ended up holding her hand.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I have to say, I have a lot of sympathy for her friend Margaret's position on all this. I totally understand that feeling of, what good is talking about this going to do. What can words possibly do here against the enormity of this awfulness? Or on the flip side, how can words possibly capture all I feel for you?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our program, people who find themselves in situations where the words really do not seem to capture what's happening. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, The Speaking Part.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So this is a story of a woman who ran out of words, just stopped talking or close to it. It took 72 days, exactly 72 days. Chana Joffe-Walt tells what happened.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The first time I talked to Youmna, it was a couple of months ago. And we mostly talked about her four kids, the questions they were asking her, and how she was answering those questions. There was her youngest, Joury, Juju, who had become obsessed with talking about her cat. The family left the cat when they fled their home in Gaza City on October 13, six days after Hamas attacked Israel.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Juju wanted to know, was the cat getting food? Yes, Youmna said. The neighbors were feeding her. There was Mohammed, 11 years old, who, two weeks into the war, had begun pulling at his lips and biting into them until the skin tore. Mohammed wanted to know if his school was still there. Yes, Youmna said. Cerine, 8 years old. Every time the family fled, she always wanted to know where they would sleep, and would they be able to sleep together? Yes, Youmna would reassure her. We will all sleep right next to each other.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The trickiest was Aline, Youmna's oldest, her 12-year-old.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Aline is always worried about her friends, especially that she can't reach them. She tells me sometimes, I don't want to call them because when they don't answer, it means that maybe they're not OK. Maybe something bad has happened to them. And I think that this is the most idea that scares her. And that's why she doesn't even try to most of the time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I talked to Aline a little bit about this, too.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Here, let me give you Aline.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Thank you.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Say hello.

segments.speaker: Aline
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Aline told me she has five close friends. They're a crew.

segments.speaker: Aline
segments.text: I called them, but they don't have signals.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: So you can't keep in touch.

segments.speaker: Aline
segments.text: So I don't know anything about them. So I have a friend. She has a little brother. He's two month, years-- he's two months just. So he's so baby. They are now staying in a car, in their car. I told her, so you don't have any cousins? You don't have any aunts in Rafah? You should go to them.

segments.speaker: Aline
segments.text: So she told me, yes, I have, but the car does not have fuel, so I can't go. But after that, she didn't call me or send me any messages or answer me to my messages. So I can't do anything now.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: So she told me, maybe something bad has happened to her. What if something bad has happened to her? I told her we would have heard. If something bad has happened to her, we would have heard. I would have known.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They seemed like the right words to say, even if Youmna had no idea if they were true. With Aline, with all her kids, Youmna's strategy was to sell them on her own certainty, even if there was no reliable information on who was dead or who was alive. She wanted them to believe there was, and she had it. Youmna would summon all the authority she had as a mom who knows things.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And Youmna is a journalist. She reports for Al Jazeera English in Gaza. So she hoped Aline would look at her, someone who has spent almost a decade tracking down records and information, and believe that of course Youmna would know if her best friend was dead.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I tell her, like we know by the families. When family is killed at bombardment, the names of those people killed are all out in a report. And I would have seen the names. I would have told you about it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Would you have told her?

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: No, I wouldn't. Definitely not. I mean, considering the problem is that the area that Dima, her best friend, was in, that's Hamad City. There were so many casualties, so many people killed there, so many people injured. And honestly, I don't know what else to tell her. I don't want her-- I don't want her to have that thought. Aline breaks down a lot. She's the eldest, and she understands more.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: But even the younger kids were understanding more than Youmna wanted them to as the war went on. They were starting to worry about everything that was happening in the parts of their world they could no longer see. What was still standing, their school, their cat, their friends. And Youmna just kept trying to convince them, it's all still there.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I don't think they really believed me, because sometimes they tell me, how would you know? And Mohammed had a friend from a Saa family, and so he heard that the Saa family was killed in one of the airstrikes. And he came and he asked me, do you think that Yamin was killed too with his family, or did he survive? And I said, it's probably not Yamin's family. It's probably another family with the same name. He's probably somewhere safe. You don't have to worry about it.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: So I try to, but-- and then he just stopped asking. He doesn't ask me about anything anymore. And neither does Aline.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I think they just-- it's either they're not convinced by the answers, or they just feel that they don't want to know.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The kids' fear of what might happen to people they couldn't see began to turn toward the family and apply to Youmna and her husband too. When Youmna went out reporting, her kids begged her to stay home, and not just home, but in the same room right next to them. They wanted all six family members together. They didn't want to let anyone out of sight.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Youmna told me they'd repeatedly ask a question I'd heard other parents from Gaza talk about too. Her kids would ask her, if we die, will we die together? At first, a week, 10 days into the war, Youmna would wave them off. You're not going to die. Then after a month passed, her answer changed to, you're always safe if you're in mommy's arms. Until finally, after more than 50 days of war, Youmna landed on this answer, yes, we will all six die together.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: As soon as she said it, she could see her kids were relieved. It was the one thing she could say that she could tell was actually comforting to them. That's where things were for Youmna and her family. 61 days into the war, they'd relocated five times. The kids were asking harder questions, except some questions which they'd stopped asking altogether. Words were more and more difficult, but not yet impossible.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Then there was a shift. Youmna and her husband got word that she had permission to leave Gaza with the kids, but not with her husband. Youmna's parents and siblings are in Egypt. She has Egyptian citizenship. The kids do too, but her husband does not, even though they've been married 15 years. Immediately when they got this news, Youmna's husband, Selah, started lobbying her.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: He was telling me, you might have to take the kids out to safety. You have to take them. This is the fifth time that we have evacuated. He told me, just take the kids and leave.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Youmna told him no. She couldn't bear it. No, he said. You have to go. You have to take the kids out. It was late. They thought they were talking quietly, but Aline, their 12-year-old, was always listening.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Yes, she actually heard her dad telling me to just take the kids and to save them. And she was-- she just screamed, Dad, what are you saying? We're not going anywhere without you, and we're not going to leave you here. We're not going to leave without you. What if something happens to you? And he even told her, Aline, this is our call. We decide. We're your parents. And she was like, no, you don't get to decide this. We are not going to leave you. No one is going to leave you.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They let it alone until morning. They had a week to decide. Their names would be on a list at the border for that week, and then the window would close. When I talked to Youmna, it was the middle of that week. At night, they debated, Youmna and Selah whispering after the kids went to sleep. And during the day, Youmna would quietly turn everything over in her head. Should she take the kids and leave him? Could she?

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: For me and my husband, we fell in love, and we got married. It wasn't just a regular marriage or anything. We're from two different nationalities and two different worlds. And we had this really nice relationship, and we made a nice family, and we traveled here and there. And he's just-- he's a part of me. He's a part of my heart. I can't just leave him. If I would leave him, I'd be ripping a part of my heart apart.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Even if it might save your kids' lives?

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I'm not going to lie to you and tell you, no, I didn't think like that. Of course I did.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I did. But I felt the guilt to even think like that because he's part of us. He's a part of me.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They talked about it for a week, and then their time was up. Youmna told me she had made a decision. They were staying. All six of them stick together. That was it.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I didn't hear from Youmna for a while. There were communication blackouts in Gaza, no electricity. But I could see she was out reporting, interviewing kids in camps, who told her their stomachs ached from hunger, talking to women living in tents who are trying to manage their periods without menstrual supplies. And then on December 21, I was surprised to see a post from Youmna saying she was in Egypt.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Hello.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi, Youmna.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Hey.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Hi.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I'm really sorry it took me a lot of time to answer you, but it has been really a very difficult time.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She said, in the middle of the month, her kids had started going hungry. Juju, her youngest, had stopped asking for food altogether because she knew there wasn't any. The phones were in and out. There was almost no internet. They had very little contact with the outside world. And then one night, Youmna got a call.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: 9:00 PM. On Wednesday, 9:00 PM, my dad found a way, and he connected with me. And he told me that you are-- your names are all on a list, and you need to travel tomorrow morning. You need to leave because your names are on a list.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Her father had gotten them back on the list of people who had permission to leave Gaza and enter Egypt. They had another short window of time to leave. But her husband, Selah, was still not on the list. Selah immediately pushed, harder than he had the last time.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: He said, it's a message from God that you need to leave with the kids. This is the right choice now. You need to save yourself now.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: The three other families Youmna and Selah were living with, they joined in too.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Youmna, you need to go. Just go. We're all waiting for that chance. We're waiting to be able to travel. You're not doing anything wrong. The wrong thing is that you would stay here.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: And her parents from Egypt.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Youmna, you need to think about the kids. My mom, she told me, the kids, they're a gift from God, and you need to protect that gift.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What actually changed things for Youmna was when her dad called back and said, take Selah with you to the border. I've spoken with them. They will let him through, even without an Egyptian passport. They've given me their word. Go. Youmna wasn't sure if there really was a promise or if everyone just wanted her to do as they said. But she started packing.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: So we went to the border. The Palestinian side was telling my husband that his name is not on the list and that he can't cross with us. So I told them, we're not going to cross if you don't let him cross, and he's a father. What about these children? They need their father. I need my husband with us.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They told her, you'll just get to the Egyptian side, and they'll send him back. So let them send him back, Youmna said. Don't you stop us. So the Palestinian guards let her family cross to the Egyptian side, where they sat and waited for eight hours. Her husband, Selah, sat right next to her, whispering into her ear nonstop. Youmna, are you listening to me? Youmna, you have to go without me.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: And he was literally the eight hours just telling me that I need to leave. I can't go back with him. I need to save our kids' lives. He reminded me how much we have struggled with water, how much we struggle with food. What are you going to do if we end up moving in tents? How are we going to keep them warm? How are we going to keep them safe with no toilets, with no water? He told me, I'm going to be OK. I'm one person. If I don't eat, it's OK. If I don't find enough water, it's fine. I'm an adult.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: How were you feeling during that time, Youmna, when you--

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I felt like it was really-- it was really surprising. I felt deeply in my heart that he's going to cross with us. It's going to be OK. I just told him, don't worry, don't worry. I know it's going to be OK. And he was like, OK, OK. Inshallah, it's going to be OK, but are you focusing with me?

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: You need to go. Are you listening to what I'm saying? You need to go. He was telling me that this is the only choice that we have for us to continue saving their lives. So eight hours later, they actually just called our names and gave us our passports, all of us, with no problems at all.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They passed through, made it to Egypt, all of them.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: So when we just entered my dad's home in Egypt, my husband, he got into the room, and he broke down, and he cried. And he cried so hard, like he cried his heart off.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: And I just looked at him, and I closed the door. I just told him, you know what, I think you should cry. You need to cry.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Had you seen him cry like that before?

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Never. Never seen him cry like that. I was really hoping that I could do the same, but I just wish I could. But I just felt like I just-- I just want to be quiet.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When she got online, Youmna saw that Al Jazeera was reporting her cameraman, Samer Abu Daqqa, had just been killed by an Israeli drone strike. She said nothing and didn't cry. She saw messages from the families they'd been living with in Rafah. They told her, right after she left, an airstrike had landed so close to the house that all the windows shattered.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Meanwhile, in her parents' home, all around her, everyone was busy, her kids, her husband. They were re-entering the world, reacting to everything, to the food and beds and lights.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: My dad was telling me Juju, my five-year-old, Juju, come on let's take a shower. And she told him, there's no water to shower. And he was like, no, we have water here. And he told her to come look. He took her to the bathroom, and he opened the tap. And water came out, and she was very excited. She was like, oh, they have water.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: And he told her, we have hot water too. And she was like, Mommy, Mommy, they have water in the shower. They have water in the tap. And my dad, he like-- he cried. He hugged her, and he cried. He told her, I'm sorry. I'm so sorry that you lived all this. And every single detail went on like that. Oh, my God, you have this. Oh, my God, you have that. Oh, my God, I miss this so much. Even the simple things and food and drink and so on.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: When Juju was like, oh, my God, water, and she was excited, and your dad started crying, how did she respond to seeing her grandfather cry?

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Well, she cried too. He was hugging her, and she cried too. And then he cried so hard. I felt like it was easy for everyone to actually cry and bring out their emotions, and even the kids and everything. But I wasn't even able to bring that out.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Youmna's family was safe. She was safe. She was suddenly one of very few people who had experienced the war and was now about to start living on the other side of it, the after. It was 72 days into the war, and that day, Youmna stopped speaking. Aside from the bare minimum basic instructions to her kids, yes, no, Youmna stopped saying anything at all. It went on like that for a week, her first week in Egypt. When we talked, this conversation, it was two weeks after she'd arrived.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: No, I wasn't talking. Literally, I was not speaking, not even to my mom, not to my dad. I just felt like I can't just-- I can't talk. I have nothing to say.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Wow.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I don't know. The only thing that I felt is like I have this very strong, very big, heavy concrete sheet over my chest that's just blocking everything. It felt like I could hardly breathe.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: She wasn't able to sleep either or eat.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: A lot of people from my family and my work, everywhere, everyone was telling me that I need to see a therapist, that I need to start therapy. And actually, my organization was really pushing me towards it, that they even got me someone. But I literally just opened the laptop, and I slammed it back because he just kept on asking me questions, like, how do you feel, what do you want to say. I didn't have the ability to bring out words from my mouth.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Because words feel-- they feel wrong when you're like--

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Because words feel very, very simple and very light. They're not describable enough to what I feel, to the thoughts that I have in my head. There are things until now that I can't speak to anyone about. Even I don't allow myself to think of, because if I do think about them, I won't be able to be normal.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I've seen kids in pieces. I've seen that. I've seen it with my own eyes. I don't want to express these things because if I do let them out, I express them. Then I start dealing with their consequences.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: What broke the logjam for Youmna to start speaking was an invitation to lunch. A week after they'd arrived in Egypt, she and her husband visited a family of Palestinians they knew from Gaza, who are now in Egypt. They all sat, ate food, and she talked. They talked about neighborhoods, places they shared in common, people they knew, and flour, what it was like over the last many weeks to try to find flour.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: They didn't talk about the most brutal or scary things they'd witnessed. They talked about the world they'd shared together in Gaza. That's what did it. And when Youmna got back to her parents' house, she kept talking. And she tried to share that world with her family, to tell them what it had been like in Gaza, what she'd seen.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Once I start speaking about some details, these details, they can't stand the picture of it. They can't stand the fact that we were too thirsty, and there was no water.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Or we were very hungry, and there was no food. We weren't able to get food or to find food. So they would interrupt you, and they would be like, oh, my God. Oh, my God. OK, this has ended. This has gone. And then they would even-- they would even cry to that story. Right? And you just feel like you haven't even-- you haven't even said anything about all this.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Youmna was speaking, but she could never get anywhere.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: I talked to Youmna one more time after this, mid-January. And she told me the day before, she had gone to therapy in person. And apparently, she talked the entire time. It was just a stream of a million thoughts and feelings in no particular order. And as she talked, she noticed there was one particular feeling she kept circling back to.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I told him I have a lot of rage inside. I just feel angry. Every time it rains, I'm angry. My friends are living in tents in this cold. These little kids now in tents, they're getting wet. Their tents are sinking in the mud.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: People shopping in the market in Egypt made Youmna mad, people going to work, her family.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: I told my sister once, she was telling me that I-- this happened in New Year's Eve. She told me, I want to go out and celebrate New Year's Eve. You want to come with me? And I just snapped. I told her, you're going to celebrate New Year's Eve? People are being killed. How can you say that? And I got really angry.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: And she was like, oh, I'm joking. I'm not going anywhere. I'm joking, dear. It's OK. And I felt for a second like-- I'm not normally that fast-tempered or bad-tempered person. But I just felt like, what the hell? What are you saying? So she was like, no, I'm just joking.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: Was she joking?

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: She wasn't joking. But the fact that I snapped about it and I felt really hurt about it made her say that she's joking, and she actually didn't go anywhere. So I don't even know if that's right or wrong. I don't know. Come on. I told her, if I was there, would you be celebrating? And that's where it ends for them. I'm back. My family's back. So for them, this has ended. The big suffering has ended.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: In some ways for you, this has ended.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: This has never ended for me, not even a bit. Not even a bit. I don't feel that it has even ended a bit. I spend most of my day watching what's happening in Gaza, watching the news about Gaza, watching videos. So for me, definitely no. I'm not living like someone who's in Gaza, and I'm not living like someone who's in Egypt now.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: You're like a ghost.

segments.speaker: Youmna
segments.text: Exactly. I'm constantly thinking about what's happening there. I don't feel like going anywhere. I don't feel like interacting with anyone. I don't even feel like talking to people, and I just want to spend this time looking at what's happening in Gaza.

segments.speaker: Chana Joffe-Walt
segments.text: That's where Youmna is more than 100 days into the war. When she does talk, most of the time what comes out is rage.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Chana Joffe-Walt is a producer on our show. Coming up, a mother reads her teenage daughter's diary. And the things she confronts her about, the thing that upsets, her choice of words. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This American Life. I'm Ira's Glass. Today's show, "The Words to Say It," we have stories today about situations where words fail to get at what is really happening. We have arrived at Act 2 of our show. Act 2, Toska.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When Valerie Kipnis was growing up, there was one word that her mother just did not want to use, even if it seemed like the right word for the situation. This went on for years, and it was a real puzzle for Val. Here she is.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: When I was 10 years old, in the fourth grade, my guidance counselor called Mama in to see her. It was urgent, she said. I knew why she had called in Mama. It was most definitely because of my nearly failing grade on a geography quiz. I should have just told my mother.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I sat outside the office, ear pressed against the splintered wood door.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Has anything happened in the home recently?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Has there been any family trouble?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Perhaps you can remember a triggering event from her past or present.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Again, no.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Any familial history of mental illness?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Of course not.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Is there a history of physical abuse?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: What? No.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Why the bruises then?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: A snort. Gymnastics. Why must you Americans always assume the worst? She does gymnastics.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Well, I apologize for asking. It's just that the state requires that I do. Still, may I suggest some sort of counseling or therapy for her? It could be helpful. It's not particularly normal for 10-year-olds to write this way. Mrs. D is concerned. I am concerned. We're all concerned. Here's a list of some good counselors in the South Brooklyn area if you decide to seek help, which we, again, recommend.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Yes, OK. Thank you, Mrs. Guidance Counselor. Appreciate your time, Mrs. Counselor, Mama said in her fractured English.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: On the walk home, Mama said nothing. She marched quickly in her burgundy crocodile print pointy-toed leather heels, clutching a paper the counselor had given her. It was not my geography quiz. It was a creative writing assignment about trees for my living environment class. The last run-on sentence was, "I am hollow and dead and alive all at the same time. How am I any different than a tree stuck in a permanent fall?"

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: As we walk through our apartment building's metal gates, Mama addressed me in Russian. Look at me, she said. Are you sad, Lera? No, I'm fine, Mama. Your stupid counselor seems to think you are depressed, she said as she opened the door to our apartment, gesturing with her fingers to make quotation signs in the air around the word "depressed."

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: What a stupid American word. How can a child be depressed? You have everything. You can be sad for a little, sure, but you are not depressed. Bozhe moi, these Amerikantzi are so dramatic. My mother yelled out to my father, Marik, do you think children can be depressed? In America, my father shouted from the bedroom. No, they have everything. What do they have to be depressed about? Exactly like I said, Mama responded, satisfied.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: We arrived in the US when I was one. Immigration defined the first decade of my life. Cans of tuna for dinner, ESL classes, and small, often crowded living spaces. I didn't speak English fluently until I was eight. By the time I was in the sixth grade, I had shed my thick Russian accent and the last two letters of my first name, Valeriya. I went by Valerie now, Val for short.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: My grandmothers deemed me an Amerikanka. That meant I took phone calls with Con Edison, instructed landlords how to fix our oftentimes broken radiators, and negotiated rates for vacation timeshares. I could be a moody child, self-serious, sometimes sad in ways that felt too big for my body. Mostly, I kept this to myself. But occasionally, my feelings would slip out, like one day when I was 15.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I came home from dance practice to find my diary open on the marble-topped island in our kitchen, my mother crying. Lera, come sit next to me, pozhaluysta. Throwing down my backpack, I settled myself on the stool next to her. Lera, Lerachka, why do you write this way? Scrawled in seafoam green jelly pen, my handwriting read, "There is no meaning to it all. I would end it, but that would hurt everyone around me." The words now felt foreign.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Because it's how I feel. I write what I feel. That's the point of having a diary, Mama. It's private. Why would you look through it? Why?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: What are these negative thoughts? Why do you have such feelings? Tell me, Lera, please. Is this coming from the TV you watch? I knew your father should not have installed that stupid cable.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: From cable? Really, Mama? You think Hannah Montana is making me depressed?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Again, with that word, "depressed." She let the syllables roll thick out of her mouth. You are not depressed, Lera. You simply cannot be. This feeling is momentary. You are a teenager. It is hormones. It happens to everybody. OK, you are sad. Sure. But it will be over tomorrow.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: In true teen fashion, I yelled, you don't understand. I hate you. Then ran into my room, slammed the door, buried my face in a pillow, and cried. I wished I could reveal her inadequacy as a mother, to hurt her by really ending it. But even alone in my room, I could hear her voice in the back of my mind, shaming me. We immigrate here for you, and this is what you do to us. You are not depressed. You're a selfish little girl. This was my mother's power. She could wear me down, even if she was only inside my head.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And this was how it went. I could be sad, but not depressed. I could be nervous, but not anxious. I could be particular, but not obsessive. Therapy and medication were completely out of the question. But maybe she was right. My job as the immigrant daughter was to be grateful, to be content.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I grew up. I moved out. And then a month before I turned 25, I stopped being able to take full breaths. At first, small, enclosed spaces like elevators made me anxious. Within a few months, I'd stop taking the subway. Then obsessive thoughts kicked in. I moved apartments, and when I couldn't adjust to my new home, I began to walk the Williamsburg Bridge at night to my old place. I still had the keys.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I would sit on the floor of the vacant apartment for hours. I did this for a month before I realized that I should perhaps seek help. My therapist-- I'll call her Terry-- had pink hair and worked from an office with another therapist's name on the door. It was kind of confusing, but she was cheap. She certified that I was depressed and anxious with OCD-like tendencies, more O than C, she said.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I was sort of proud, to have a word. It felt real. I decided to tell my parents that I was seeing a therapist. I told them one night in the car. I thought maybe they would be concerned or ask questions, but it was like they didn't hear me. Except I heard my mother mutter in Russian, Amerikanskaya chyzh, meaning American nonsense.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And just like that, my mother's voice was back inside my head. Whenever Terry told me I was depressed, instead of feeling relieved or understood, I wanted to argue. I wanted to yell. Really, depressed? Good one, Terry. Maybe I'm just sad today. Can't a person be sad? Stop diagnosing me.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: But I didn't actually yell any of this. Instead, I would nod and let her tell me about coping mechanisms, such as yoga and journaling, a healthier diet, vitamin D. Chekhov once wrote, "If many remedies are prescribed for an illness, you may be certain that the illness has no cure." And whenever Terry would prescribe self-care to deal with my never-ending sadness, I would think about my parents. I would think about toska.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: OK, a word about toska. For most Russians of my parents' generation, there was no real word for depression. The word they did say was toska. After I gave up on Terry, I started googling around, hoping to understand why my mom was so uncomfortable with the word "depression." And here's what I learned.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: It goes back to the Soviet era. During that time, mental illness was stigmatized, seen as a problem that only afflicted capitalist societies, a problem that would disappear under Communist rule. The model Soviet citizen, a tovarish, could not be mentally ill. My father once told me there could be no depression in the world we were building because we were striving for this perfection.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: They did use the word "depresiya," but it felt like a foreign import. And anyway, it was reserved for those in the highest rung of emotional distress, those who had lost a spouse in war or a child at birth, and not much else. And there was another much more menacing way Soviets talked about mental illness, and that was as a political weapon. Political and cultural dissidents were pronounced mentally ill, unsound of mind, and locked up in psychiatric hospitals.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: It was a very dark Soviet logic. You couldn't be mentally ill and be a model Soviet citizen. But at the same time, if you were not a model Soviet citizen, well, the reason for that was, you were mentally ill. And if you were just a person who wanted to see a psychiatrist, like people did in the West, well, therapy was essentially banned by Soviet authorities for three generations.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Every person who received psychiatric treatment, even just a consultation, was registered by the state. After that, it could be difficult to apply for work or keep jobs. Whatever psychiatry did exist was mostly underground. Mostly things stayed this way until the 1990s, until the Soviet Union fell apart.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Now, things are different. But for people like my parents who left just a few years after that, mental illness remained taboo. They had different words to talk about these sorts of feelings, words like "toska." "Toska" is a word Russians consider to be, in its essence, Russian. It is both of them and for them. It's one of the things that defines the Russian soul, which is perhaps why it is so untranslatable.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I think Vladimir Nabokov captures toska's meaning best. "No single word in English renders all the shades of toska. At its deepest and most painful, it is a sensation of great spiritual anguish, often without any specific cause. At less morbid levels, it is a dull ache of the soul, a longing with nothing to long for, a sick pining, a vague restlessness, mental throes, yearning."

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Toska and depression share some things in common, but they are not the same. Like, depression is the lack of desire, while toska is the desire for something unattainable. Toska is not a diagnosis. It is a collective sense of loss. It is a heavy weight. It is the darkness of long winters. "Toska" is the word my mother always used to describe her first decade in America. Bilo ochen tosklivo. It was filled with toska.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Mama describes her first months in New York as horrific. The story goes like this. When we arrived at JFK, she took one look around and immediately started crying. We moved into an apartment on Avenue P in Brooklyn. It felt like my soul had been ripped out of my human, my mother once told me. I stopped seeing life in color. Everything about New York seemed awful and gray.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: She was a 28-year-old refugee with a one-year-old. She became obsessed with the past. She forgot about the poverty that accompanied the fall of the Soviet Union, the lawlessness, the gang violence, the dead bodies she herself had walked past in the street. Mama said, I could only think of the beauty, the canals. I could only think of my mother.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: She spent hours walking around South Brooklyn with me in a carriage and her Walkman on full blast, listening mostly to Alexander Rosenbaum, a Russian folk singer known for his lyrics about prison confinement, Leningrad, suffering, and tortured love. She would play her favorite song, "Naletela Grust," Sadness Has Descended Onto Me, on repeat. I imagine her cold fingers-- not yet swollen from the houses she'll clean, the toilets she will scrub-- reach for protruding plastic buttons. Pause, rewind, play.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: During her first year in America, my mother lived in almost total solitude. My father was in school during the day and working as a dishwasher in a Burrow Park restaurant by night. For company, she had only me, a crying baby. Mama said, I felt unnecessary in this country. I felt unnecessary to myself. I was an adult woman with an engineering degree, and here I was sitting at home all day, not knowing how to ask for directions or buy food if I was starving. I felt like I might as well just roll over and die. She'd say, Tosklivo bilo mne. Toska had come over me.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: For a long time, I felt like "toska" was a word that belonged to my mother, but not to me. I felt like I didn't deserve to take on a feeling from a place where I'd only spent a year of my life. It felt fraudulent to equate my puny American miserableness with the great Russian toska. I wasn't Russian enough to feel toska, and I didn't deserve to feel depression. Despite having two languages at my disposal, I had no word to cling to.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: And then something happened. I was with my mother at home in her kitchen. We talked as she waited for holodetz to solidify. And I asked her a question I used to ask all the time as a little girl. I asked her to tell me the story of how we got here. And she told that story the same way she always had, until I asked her about the days when we lived in the apartment on Avenue P, when it was mostly me and her together.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: She sighed. Her hands were covered in a sticky gelatin, so she wiped her brow with the inside of her wrist. Oh, Lera, those were the hardest years of my life. It felt like the shadow had come over me. I definitely felt toska, but it was also, well, probably depression, she told me. It was so casual, so effortless, the way she just said "depression" as if it was nothing, as if it was a word she had been saying all her life.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I could see her reflection in the mirror of the microwave, and she didn't even hesitate, just kept on cooking. I sat behind her stunned. Did that just happen? A few weeks later, we were on the phone, and I could tell she was in a strange mood. So I asked how she was doing. Depressed, Lera. I'm feeling depressed, she said. Jeez.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: This time, I was angry. This is a word she's just using now? Why did she get to use the word she had always denied to me? Did she even have the right to use the word, to redefine her life so late in the game? I resisted the urge to say something cruel.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Months passed, and I began to realize that I had spent so long feeling that I did not deserve to be depressed that now, I was not allowing my mother to be depressed either. It took me a while to get the courage to finally ask her about it. Why was she suddenly OK with this word? She shrugged. What did you expect? I didn't know what the word really meant until recently. How was I to know that's what I was experiencing?

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Coming into this knowing, it wasn't a big moment for her. It was a bunch of smaller ones. She started hearing more Russian speakers use the word in America, on Russian-language TV. She unattached the meaning of that Soviet depresiya from depression. And over time, the word just lost its stigma.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: I didn't think I could feel depression as an immigrant, she said. I thought I could have only been toska. I think if she had said she was depressed, then she'd be admitting defeat as an immigrant. She would be admitting that even here in America, after leaving her home to give her children a better life, things could still feel bad. And all those times my mother told me depression was an American concept-- that I wasn't sick, but just particular, that my mood was temporary or could not possibly exist because I was too privileged in America-- looking at it now, I wonder how much of that was meant for me and how much of it was for her.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: My mother wasn't wrong in describing how she felt in America as toska. But I think she didn't realize she didn't have to choose between "toska" and "depression." She could have both words. I didn't understand that either. To me, "toska" is the word that comes the closest to the feeling of being a child of immigrants, maybe better than any other word I know. It's the knowledge that no matter how hard you try, you will never see the things your family saw, that you will never understand them fully. And they will never really understand you.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: It's the yearning for a place your parents claim as home. And it's a word I finally feel is mine. These days, while my mother and I are on the phone and she's cleaning, I'll hear the way she's breathing and ask if she's OK. She'll tell me she's feeling depressed, and I'll tell her that that's OK. There's no shame in that. I feel it too.

segments.speaker: Valerie Kipnis
segments.text: Sometimes when she asks how I'm doing, I'll take an inhale, the kind that gets caught in your throat right before you start to cry. And she'll wait a minute and check I'm still there. And I'll tell her that I feel toska. And she'll say, of course you do. You're my daughter.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Valerie Kipnis, a.k.a. Valeriya, a.k.a. Lera, is a producer on our show. She's working on a memoir about immigrants and untranslatable words.
